Ubisoft dumps its money into gen AI with subsidiary Motherbrain "focused on AI for gameplay"

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (653 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gamesradar

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • While the industry debates the value of using generative AI as a behind-the-scenes development tool, Ubisoft is leaping over that fence.
  • Motherbrain "has been established as a dedicated subsidiary developing proprietary technology for latest forms of gameplay.
  • Industry observers note that ubisoft has been talking up the idea of NPCs powered by generative AI for years, going back to an effort called Project NEO NPC, which built characters that could respond to players like an LLM-powered chatbot with its own backstory.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

While the industry debates the value of using generative AI as a behind-the-scenes development tool, Ubisoft is leaping over that fence. The company has tripled down on its intention to put player-facing generative AI in its games, announcing the establishment of a new subsidiary called Motherbrain, which is "focused on AI for gameplay innovation.".

Motherbrain "has been established as a dedicated subsidiary developing proprietary technology for latest forms of gameplay. Its current focus is on new player experiences, smart NPCs with memory and AI game masters that manage large-scale systemic worlds," Ubisoft says in its latest financial report. "It aims to serve creators globally, both within Ubisoft’s Creative House ecosystem and beyond, and form partnerships with selected technology actors.".

Industry observers note that ubisoft has been talking up the idea of NPCs powered by generative AI for years, going back to an effort called Project NEO NPC, which built characters that could respond to players like an LLM-powered chatbot with its own backstory. By 2025, that effort had evolved into Teammates, a prototype shooter built around a squad of companions that respond to "real-time voice commands" and "adapt their behavior to each situation, revealing distinct personalities along the way.".

In a recent development, now, the Teammates devs are now heading Motherbrain. Ubisoft CEO Yves Guillemot hopes that Motherbrain's work will "open up new possibilities for richer, more immersive and engaging player experiences.".

It has been revealed that all this comes amid mass layoffs at Ubisoft. The company claims its headcount was down to 15,500 as of September 2026. That's an eye-watering number in itself, but it's a massive reduction in people from 20,700 in September 2022. Ubisoft says it's cut 1,100 jobs in the past six months alone.

The extent to which AAA developers are already using generative AI to create games is not fully clear to us on the outside, though certainly there are people, like Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, who are keen to suggest it's already nigh-ubiquitous. But AI generating in-game content live for players is much rarer, outside of Epic's own AI Darth Vader, which instantly started spouting slurs.

Back in 2025, Guillemot presented his own vision for games with built-in AI content generation. "For players, the world will react to their behavior instead of pre-scripted things," he mentioned. "We have been creating open worlds in the past, giving more choices to payers, and now we will go another step further, which is, OK, [to] make sure that you have an impact on the world, and the world will react to you. So it will be your world.".

Weekly digests, tales from the communities you love, and more.

Some players will look at the possibility of a game world with infinite, responsive content as something magical. Personally? I've played several of Ubisoft's 100-hour open-world epics to completion, and I know even human developers can struggle to populate these worlds with engaging stories and things to do. It's tough to imagine a chatbot version of Socrates offering an experience worth remembering.

As it lays off another 166 developers, Ubisoft notes Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced is "among the industry's most successful action-adventure remakes".

Dustin Bailey joined the GamesRadar team as a Staff Writer in May 2022, and is right now based in Missouri. He's been covering games (with occasional dalliances in the worlds of anime and pro wrestling) since 2015, first as a freelancer, then as a news writer at PCGamesN for nearly five years. His love for games was sparked somewhere between Metal Gear Solid 2 and Knights of the Old Republic, and these days you can usually find him splitting his entertainment time between retro gaming, the latest major action-adventure title, or a long haul in American Truck Simulator.

Industry News: 10 Google Privacy Hacks Everyone Should Know

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (982 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, from managing your Gmail inbox to downloading apps on your Android phone, pretty much every aspect of your digital life has a little bit of Google in it.
  • Recent findings suggest that your Gmail account doesn't just have one email address.
  • It has been revealed that if you wish to make your emails more private, you can also link your Proton Mail account to Gmail.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, from managing your Gmail inbox to downloading apps on your Android phone, pretty much every aspect of your digital life has a little bit of Google in it. That is a lot of power in the hands of a tech giant that makes money by selling your data to advertisers. While you can't fully escape Google's tracking without quitting a whole bunch of essential online services, you can use these privacy hacks to reduce how the company tracks you, as well as protect the information in your Google account.

Recent findings suggest that your Gmail account doesn't just have one email address. In fact, it has unlimited addresses, but you need a hack to utilize them. When you're signing up for a new service, you can add another word to your email address, as well as the "+" symbol, to create an alias. For example, if your email is "[email protected]," and you're signing up for an Amazon account, you can use "[email protected]" as your email address. The email will still end up in your main inbox, as if you simply used [email protected]. Not only can this trick turn one Gmail address into an unlimited number of addresses, but it also helps you identify who sold your email address to spammers, because those emails will have the alias in the "To" field.

It has been revealed that if you wish to make your emails more private, you can also link your Proton Mail account to Gmail. This lets you send and receive emails via your Gmail address, while using Proton Mail's privacy protections such as blocking email trackers.

In a recent development, google wants to show you personalized search results, which initially feels very helpful, but it also ends up trapping you in an algorithmic bubble. The best way to break out of your search bubble is to periodically use other search engines, but if you wish to stick to Google, you can disable personalized search recommendations in Google Search and the Play Store on Android. Go to this settings page, and turn off Personalized Recommendations and Play Personalization.

Industry observers note that google tracks your web and app activity by default, which includes your search history, voice data (if you use the speak-to-search feature), and activity from sites, apps, and devices that use Google services. However, associated information, such as your location data, is also saved to your Google profile, which you might not assume gets included in "Web & app activity." Fortunately, you can disable this tracking by going to this settings page, scrolling down to "Web & App Activity," and turning off all options in this section.

Google's Timeline feature saves your location in Google Maps to create a map of places you've visited. This is useful if you want to keep track of your recent stops; however, Google can use Timeline data to help businesses see how effective their ads were, or how likely you are to visit nearby stores. Its confirmation page confirms this: "Depending on your settings, activity saved as history in your Google Account, including ad interactions, may also be connected to Timeline data to help nearby businesses estimate the likelihood that people will visit their stores. No personal information is shared with businesses.".

Recent findings suggest that timeline isn't enabled by default, but in case you enabled it a while ago, and are no longer using it, you can turn it off by going to this settings page. Click Turn off, and delete your activity to remove Timeline data from your Google account.

Industry observers note that you can't fully escape Google's ads or tracking, but you can disable personalized ads to stop the company from using your account data to show ads. To do this, go to this settings page, and turn off Personalized ads.

While Google claims that it isn't using your emails to train AI, the organization does offer AI features that make your emails feel more robotic than human. One of these is "Smart Reply," which offers email reply suggestions such as "Got it. See you soon." I can type that on my own, and I feel uncomfortable with Gmail analyzing the contents of my emails and replies to offer suggestions that I wouldn't use anyway. You can disable this by going to Gmail Settings > General, or by visiting this settings page. Scroll down to "Smart features," and turn off the checkbox next to it. This will disable Smart Compose, Smart Reply, suggestions for pending replies and follow-ups, spelling, grammar, and autocorrect.

Industry observers note that A physical security key is a great security upgrade. It's a physical barrier that prevents most ways to hack into your account remotely. Even if someone discovers your email ID and password, and has access to your two-factor authentication code, they won't get in without physical access to that key. You can check out Google's support page for physical security keys for more information on compatibility and setting up your security keys.

If you're serious about your online privacy and security, I'd advise against keeping your primary credit card saved to your Google account. If your account is compromised or your device is stolen, you risk exposing your credit card to fraud. Instead, use a prepaid virtual card with your Google account. Sites such as Privacy.com offer single-use or merchant-locked prepaid cards, and they allow you to set spending limits too. You can use such services with your Google account to reduce the chances of losing money if your account gets hacked.

Recent findings suggest that google uses data from Gmail and Google Drive to target ads, which means that your emails, files, and photos could be used for monetization. To stop this, you'll need to disable Personal Intelligence. To turn it off, visit this settings page, and click Turn off Personal Intelligence.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that last Monday morning was an exciting time for fans of British spy thrillers. First, Slow Horses was renewed for Seasons 9 and 10, meaning we’ll be getting at least four more seasons of the hit show, available with an Apple TV subscription. Then, just hours later, Amazon MGM finally dropped the bomb we've all been waiting for and announced that the next actor to play James Bond would be Robert Pattinson. Many of us had been waiting for that for months. Years, even, yet it still came as a surprise, given the latest rumors. In hindsight, I probably should have been clued in that the announcement was imminent after the Slow Horses news dropped.

Over the last few weeks and months, there have been a ton of rumors regarding the next Bond ahead of the long-awaited Bond 26 finally beginning production (we’re still not sure when that will actually happen). Names like Jacob Elordi, Henry Cavill, Callum Turner, and more have been rumored. Slow Horses star Jack Lowden was also heavily rumored in recent weeks. Lowden, who plays River Cartwright on the show about disgraced MI5 agents, was looking to make the jump to MI6 and become the ninth man to play Bond.

Recent findings suggest that it’s certainly possible for an actor to appear in multiple projects, but given Slow Horses' aggressive filming schedule (they have already wrapped Season 7, due next year, and are filming Season 8), it might have been a tough schedule to work out for Lowden had he been named Bond. When the next two seasons were announced, it should have clued me in that Lowden likely wasn’t going to be James Bond going forward. It’s quite possible that Apple may have actually been waiting on the Bond decision to announce it was moving forward with more seasons of Slow Horses, too. So, when the news dropped about the show's renewal, I should have known Bond’s announcement was on deck.

Interestingly, despite the announcements coming almost at the same time, there are also rumors that Lowden might not be part of Seasons 9 and 10. A report in Variety calls Lowden’s return “uncertain.” I’m not sure what to make of that. The book-to-screen adaptation has been adapting one book per season, generally. Season 6 was an exception, as it combined two books, the 6th and 7th in Mick Herron’s series Slough House. That's not all, though.

In a recent development, warning! There are some spoilers ahead from the books Slow Horses is adapted from!

Industry observers note that that would presumably mean that Season 7 will be an adaptation of book #8, Bad Actors. As fans of the TV show know, Season 6 ended on a cliffhanger with River having been poisoned by the Russian assassins. Book readers know that River spends Bad Actors on the sidelines, recovering from the assassination attempt, and doesn’t appear in the novel at all. If the show has adapted Bad Actors for Season 7, might Lowden be mostly absent? Cartwright does return in the ninth book, Clown Town, which we do know is going to be Season 8 of the show.

In a recent development, here’s where it gets interesting. As of today, Clown Town is the most recent book to be published in the Slough House series, so we don’t know what Herron or the producers intend to take the series, so all eyes are on Lowden!

Slay the Spire 2 is one of this year's best selling games despite only being available on PC, and its players are "obsessed"

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (472 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Eurogamer

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that one million copies for each month on sale, it seems.
  • That's according to estimates by Alinea Analytics industry analyst Rhys Elliott, who revealed in a LinkedIn post that those sales translate to $157.6m (~£119.6m) in revenue for the small studio.
  • Slay the Spire 2 is now the sixth best-selling 2026 release across Steam, PlayStation and Xbox.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that one million copies for each month on sale, it seems. Slay the Spire 2, Mega Crit's roguelike deckbuilder, is estimated to have sold 7.9m copies since its release in Steam Early Access in March.

That's according to estimates by Alinea Analytics industry analyst Rhys Elliott, who revealed in a LinkedIn post that those sales translate to $157.6m (~£119.6m) in revenue for the small studio.

Slay the Spire 2 is now the sixth best-selling 2026 release across Steam, PlayStation and Xbox. That is notable, as the game is only out on Steam, meaning it has sold enough copies to outpace games on platforms it's not even available on.

In a recent development, we already knew Slay the Spire 2 was one of the year's biggest releases. In its first week on sale, the game sold over 3m copies. It swiftly became March's top-selling game on Steam, beating blockbuster competition in Crimson Desert and Resident Evil Requiem. Slay the Spire 2, alongside other indie titles such as Meccha Chameleon, have helped Steam deliver another record year of revenue.

It was such a hit, even, that other indie developers felt it negatively impacted sales of their own games. Mewgenics maker Edmund McMillen recently told Eurogamer "it sucked everybody out". "The same players who liked Mewgenics, they were Slay The Spire players. So they all went woosh and right over," McMillen stated.

Slay the Spire 2 has been consistently popular with players, too, and that popularity has seemingly continued. Elliott noted the game never fell below 2.5 million active players each month since March.

Slay the Spire 2's loyal following also meant that the recently released beta patch, which added a new character, was enough to bring back millions of players. Despite only being available for players who opt into the beta branch of the game, Slay the Spire 2 more than doubled its daily active consumers to reach its highest daily player count in six months.

"Simply put: Slay the Spire 2 players are obsessed," wrote Elliott. "And it's not just a niche group of dedicated players, either. The average play time is nearly 84 hours, sure. But zooming out, 1.9 million folks have played for over 100 hours.".

Incidentally, nearly 100,000 players bought the game but never played it, which Elliott added could explain the discrepancy between player numbers and copies sold.

Looking ahead, Slay the Spire 2's road to version 1.0 is expected to be long, with several features and gameplay additions still in the works. Then there are the console ports, which have yet to be unveiled, but are very much expected.

In Eurogamer's Slay the Spire 2 early access review, Bertie Purchese called it "a deceptively familiar sequel" whose confident design and smart new additions build on what made the original work so well.

Recent findings suggest that not even a nationwide FAA ground stop could prevent movie stars from descending upon Los Angeles for the Governor Awards and Vanity Fair's first annual Screening Room this past weekend. Hosted at LACMA's brand-fresh Steve Tisch theater, actors including Matt Damon, Penélope Cruz, Pedro Pascal, Andrew Garfield, John Leguizamo, and Andrew Scott joined Q&As to discuss their films and pressing topics in the entertainment industry. AI was a major theme throughout the weekend, and not just at the screening for Artificial, as actors and directors spoke about the desire to continue making things that feel “real” and “made by humans.” Following each screening, talent mingled with guests to continue the conversations.

The weekend began with a screening of Wild Horse Nine, director Martin McDonagh's dark comedy starring John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell as CIA agents behind the initiative to overthrow the Chilean government in 1973. Following the showing, VF's Senior Hollywood Correspondent Rebecca Ford led a Q&A with McDonagh, Malkovich and Mariana di Girolamo, who also stars in the film.

According to recent reports, next up was Elsinore, which tells the story of Scottish actor Ian Charleson (played by Andrew Scott) who attempts to perform Hamlet at the National Theatre while secretly living with AIDS. In conversation with VF's Rebecca Ford, Scott, his costar Billie Piper, and writer Stephen Beresford, Scott discussed what it was like to tell Charleson's story. “I think … why the film is so moving is because [Charleson’s] not wallowing at any point. He was insanely courageous,” he mentioned.

Come Friday night, audiences gathered for a screening of the acclaimed Spanish language drama La Bola Negra, which follows several gay men whose lives are bound together by their identities, love and loss, and the looming presence of the Spanish Civil War. It stars Miguel Bernardeau, Álvaro Lafuente Calvo (the singer known as Guitarricadelafuente) in his first major acting role, Carlos Gonzalez, Milo Quifes and Penélope Cruz.

In a recent development, after the film, Ricky Martin moderated a panel conversation featuring directors Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo, and stars Cruz, Guitarricadelafuente and Bernardeau. Calvo talked about how they are all riding high on the film's positive reception. “Creating this sense of community and hearing people saying, ‘This movie changed me. It really made me understand things about me.’ The power that art has, we forget it, but then this happens and … the rest is a dream. The rest we're living is a dream.”.

Sources indicate that saturday's slate of programming began with a live recording of Vanity Fair's “Notes on a Scene” with Matt Damon, John Leguizamo and Himesh Patel, who recounted what it was like to film The Odyssey with director Christopher Nolan. Next, Seth Rogen joined Screening Room for “Scene Selection,” taking the audience through what it was like shooting Freaks and Geeks, Knocked Up, The Studio and more.

Later that afternoon, Pedro Pascal and Tony Gilroy joined the festivities following a screening of their latest film Behemoth!, which tells the story of a prodigal cellist who returns to Los Angeles and to score films after decades performing symphonic work around the country. In conversation with VF's West Coast Editor John Ross for Behemoth!, Pascal spoke about how making the film gave him “a tremendous amount of hope.” “We weren't making money on this movie. Nobody was. And you had the most expensive people involved in this film because of their talent and their experience. So there was just this purity of love in the work from every single department, and that was incredibly contagious," he said.

Sources indicate that come Saturday night, guests were eager to see Luca Guadagnino's Artificial, which follows the rise of OpenAI and a few of its pioneers: Sam Altman, Elon Musk, Ilya Sutskever and Mira Murati. Guadagnino was joined by cast members Andrew Garfield (who plays Altman), Yura Borisov (who plays Sutskever) and Monica Barbaro (who plays Murati) for a post-screening conversation with VF's Global Editorial Director Mark Guiducci. “It's key to try to understand because as Luca mentioned, these are the kids that have the reins of the future and we've somehow allowed them to just hold onto them. And we've kind of given our autonomy over or it's been taken from behind our backs,” Garfield said.

On Sunday, Cruz joined director Florian Zeller for a screening of the film Bunker, a timely film about a famous architect, played by Javier Bardem, and his wife Sofia, played by Cruz, who is asked to build a bunker for a tech giant. This sparks a rift in their marriage as the couple examines how success and monetary gain have affected their lives. Cruz, who is having a huge year with The Invite and La Bola Negra alongside this film, expressed her excitement that younger audiences are coming back to theaters and are looking for films that don't “over-explain.".

It has been revealed that the inaugural edition of Vanity Fair’s Screening Room paired this year’s most compelling films with a slate of programming that included post-screening panels and conversations with actors and filmmakers. Following the program in Los Angeles, Vanity Fair’s Screening Room will arrive in Upcoming York, where screenings and events will take place at Cherry Lane Theatre from December 4–6.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Cyclists who ride with Garmin gear can now appear as live, moving icons on the Waze driving app, and nearby drivers will receive an alert to slow down and watch for them on the road.
  • According to recent reports, for riders already using Garmin devices, opting in costs nothing and adds a fresh layer of safety, particularly on roads where drivers may not expect cyclists.
  • Riders can simply opt in once through Garmin Connect.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cyclists who ride with Garmin gear can now appear as live, moving icons on the Waze driving app, and nearby drivers will receive an alert to slow down and watch for them on the road.

According to recent reports, for riders already using Garmin devices, opting in costs nothing and adds a fresh layer of safety, particularly on roads where drivers may not expect cyclists. The feature is rolling out now, but you should be aware of its limitations.

Riders can simply opt in once through Garmin Connect. After that, sharing starts automatically when an outdoor cycling activity begins and stops when the ride ends. While a ride is underway, Waze users near the cyclist see a cyclist icon move along the road and receive a Live Cycling Alert reminding them to slow down and stay aware.

Industry observers note that the feature runs on LiveTrack, Garmin's existing live location-sharing tool, which lets friends and family follow a rider's real-time location, speed, course, and more. Garmin says this collaboration extends that peace of mind to motorists, giving them greater awareness of their surroundings.

Garmin notes its location sharing is temporary and session-based. The rider's name, identity, and route are hidden, and no personal information is shared or displayed in Waze. Drivers see only an anonymous icon and the alert.

You'll need a few things to get this feature up and running:.

A compatible Garmin Edge bike computer or Garmin watch.

A phone running Garmin Connect with a data connection.

An outdoor cycling activity (the feature doesn't apply to indoor rides).

The good news is using the feature is free: LiveTrack costs nothing on compatible Garmin bike computers and watches, and Waze is free for drivers.

This new feature is a great safety perk, but there are real-world caveats worth considering:.

Recent findings suggest that this feature is for Waze only. Alerts reach drivers only when Waze is open on their phone. Google Maps, which has far more users, is excluded, so a large portion of the drivers you share the road with won't see you this way.

It depends on your phone's signal. Your position travels from the Garmin to your phone, then to Garmin's servers, then to Waze, and finally to the driver's phone. On a patchy rural signal, a few seconds of lag could put the icon on the wrong side of a bend from where you actually are. A rider who leaves their phone at home or whose phone loses signal simply won't show up on a Waze map, as a ride without a data connection is invisible to Waze.

According to recent reports, finally, remember to treat this safety feature as an extra perk, not a guarantee. At the end of the day, it isn't a replacement for bike lights, bright clothing, and defensive riding.

videogame executive Peter Moore, known for his time at Sega, Xbox, and Electronic Arts as well as a couple of famous tattoos, has expressed hope that the launch of Grand Theft Auto 6 will provide a much-needed "shot in the arm" for the videogame industry.

Moore began with a faked photo of himself rolling up his sleeve to reveal a GTA 6 tattoo—although the photo is based on his real-world tattoo-based reveal of Grand Theft Auto 4 on Xbox 360 at E3 2006.

In a recent development, "In all seriousness, the videogame industry could really use a moment like this," Moore wrote on X after posting the image. "We've been through a challenging period. Studio closures, redundancies, cancelled projects and enormous uncertainty have taken their toll on an industry that has given so much to so many, myself included.

Sources indicate that "That's why the launch of GTA 6 feels so significant. It's more than the release of a hugely anticipated game. It's an opportunity to remind the world of the extraordinary power of this industry to create, innovate, entertain and bring people together.".

Moore's career in the game industry began at Sega, where he oversaw the launch of the Dreamcast and promptly rose to become president and chief operating officer of Sega of America. In 2003 he went to Microsoft and became its Corporate Vice President of Interactive Entertainment Business, Entertainment and Devices Division, heading up its Xbox division; in 2007 he joined EA Sports, and eventually became the organization's chief operating officer. He left the videogame business behind in 2017 to head up Liverpool FC, but it did not work out: Despite a highly successful run, club ownership did not care for his very public style of leadership, and in 2020 his contract was not renewed.

And he did indeed announce GTA 4 with a tattoo—apologies for the resolution, it was 20 years ago.

In today's message, Moore stated he's "seen this industry reinvent itself time and time again" over those years, and expressed hope that GTA 6 delivers not just commercial success but also "a much-needed shot in the arm (no pun intended…) for the entire ecosystem: developers, publishers, studios, retailers, technology partners and the next generation of creative talent.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Last night, it was revealed that Clair Obscur: Expedition 33's lead narrative designer, Jennifer Svedberg-Yen, won a BAFTA Breakthrough US award for her contribution to the hit 2025 game, which made history after winning 12 Game Award nominations last year. In the aftermath of her win, Svedberg-Yen dropped a pretty big bombshell: she's no longer with the game's developer, Sandfall Interactive.

In a recent development, "No, I left Sandfall in July, after wrapping up some final stuff for Expedition," she told Gamesbeat when asked if she's still with the organization. "We've parted ways." As to what Svedberg-Yen is doing next, she offered a cryptic answer, including talk of writing "my own projects, my own stories". She also discussed another project she's set her sights on: establishing a fund to help mentor and grow a new generation of video game narrative designers.

It has been revealed that "One of the initiatives I want to build is a narrative investment fund to focus on narrative-focused game creators, trying to bridge the gap between the seed stage and going to publishers," she explained, noting her background working in finance and how that dovetails nicely with her more recent experience as a narrative lead. "This is the chicken and egg question a lot of people face. To get money from publishers you need a demo, but to make a demo you need money. To get money you have to go to publishers. That’s an area where I would like to help a lot of these smaller creatives to get that seed funding so they can, in a way, de-risk themselves in the eyes of bigger investors.".

Her motivation for this initiative? Simply, she wants to change how the industry works. "I've discovered that quite a lot of studios don’t really know how to think about narrative, or how to integrate it into their pipelines and their processes. They tend to think it's a very narrow thing, when in fact it can influence all aspects. Part of this would also be an incubation program to help these studios develop those narrative foundations.".

In a recent development, "The strongest feeling in me right now for 2027 is I want to help," she added later. "That sounds so cheesy and idealistic. I always cringe at myself for saying it. But I don't know how else to say it and be truthful. I want to help in some way, help the industry.".

Sandfall Interactive previously said its guiding "North Star" will always be its "own personal taste", and what the team enjoys.She noted that she didn't think the studio would bow to pressure from fans to do more of the same, but instead be guided by what it thinks is best for itself, and for the series. "I've seen too many TV highlights and books be swayed trying to please a lot of people, and in the process you end up losing the heart of what's there," she noted.

In a recent development, we know that Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 is "not the end" of the franchise, and it seems that whatever happens next, it'll have at least a little bit of Svedberg-Yen's creativity instilled in it. I wish her the best for whatever her next step is.

Mindseye developer Build a Rocket Boy - founded by ex-GTA veteran - has a mountain of debt, and the main strategy for paying it back is litigation

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Beleaguered Mindseye developer Build a Rocket Boy - the manufacturer created by former Rockstar and Grand Theft Auto producer Leslie Benzies - apparently owes approximately £62 million in debt.
  • Sources indicate that this came to light in a proposal issued by Build a Rocket Boy's administrators this week (spotted by Resetera), which lists both the moneys owed (right down to a £20 charge to OpenAI) and details what went wrong, as well as what Build a Rocket Boy intends to do to recoup money to pay the debts back.
  • According to recent reports, "Prior to the Firm's entry into Administration, the directors had been investigating circumstances surrounding the commercial performance of the video game, MindsEye, which was released in 2025 following significant development investment," the administration proposal read.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Beleaguered Mindseye developer Build a Rocket Boy - the manufacturer created by former Rockstar and Grand Theft Auto producer Leslie Benzies - apparently owes approximately £62 million in debt. And a huge chunk of that appears to be owed to Chinese gaming company NetEase (£36.5m), though more than £1m appears to be owed to Benzies himself.

Sources indicate that this came to light in a proposal issued by Build a Rocket Boy's administrators this week (spotted by Resetera), which lists both the moneys owed (right down to a £20 charge to OpenAI) and details what went wrong, as well as what Build a Rocket Boy intends to do to recoup money to pay the debts back. And the manufacturer's "largest" potential asset, according to the administrators, is litigation.

According to recent reports, "Prior to the Firm's entry into Administration, the directors had been investigating circumstances surrounding the commercial performance of the video game, MindsEye, which was released in 2025 following significant development investment," the administration proposal read. "The directors formed the view that the game's commercial prospects may have been adversely affected by a coordinated campaign of negative online reviews and commentary.

"The directors subsequently received information which they considered suggested the involvement of a number of third parties in organising and funding such activity and commenced litigation against some of those parties. The directors have indicated that any such claims may be substantial in value, although the extent of any recovery remains uncertain and will be dependent upon the outcome of ongoing investigations, legal proceedings and asset recovery actions.".

Industry observers note that this tallies with the narrative spun by co-organization leader Mark Gerhard as the company waded into deep water. Gerhard blamed "organised espionage and corporate sabotage" for the studio's difficulties as multiple rounds of layoffs shredded Build a Rocket Boy. "People had their hands on the scale and deliberately tried to shape a negative narrative around the product," Gerhard mentioned.

The situation he's referring to is likely the alleged smear campaign made against the game, which Gerhand reportedly claimed in an internal meeting this year was paid for by a "substantial American firm" and then run by a UK company called Ritual Network, which apparently had influencers, journalists and staff at Build a Rocket Boy deliberately sabotage the game's release. That's according to an account of a videoed internal meeting reportedly seen by Insider Gaming earlier this year.

It has been revealed that it had nothing to do with the dire state of Mindseye when it debuted, then. Eurogamer awarded it one out of five stars, chastising its "ridiculous story, inconsistent writing, poorly designed mission scenarios, and utterly atrocious combat" in our Mindseye review.

Build a Rocket Boy was founded in 2016, and its first game, Everywhere - a sort of online gaming platform - was announced in 2022. It never materialised, but a part of that vision was carved out to become a standalone game experience of its own along the way, and that's how we got Mindseye - a take on a Grand Theft Auto formula. Whether or not the litigation is successful and can recoup any of Build a Rocket Boy's debts remains to be seen, but there's a financial mountain for the studio to climb if it hopes to operate again.

#51406. 10 Movies Like ‘Interstellar’ You Should Watch Next

Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Lifehacker ↗ Open Full Page

10 Movies Like ‘Interstellar’ You Should Watch Next

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1267 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Christopher Nolan’s 2014 megahit Interstellar has it all: substantial sci-fi ideas, cool robots, ugly crying, and a Matt Damon character in need of rescuing.
  • If you loved both the special effects in Interstellar that make space travel feel viscerally thrilling (and terrifying) and the mind-blowing concepts, this is the film for you.
  • According to recent reports, if you’re looking for more existential missions with somewhat reluctant heroes in space, Project Hail Mary is your next stop.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Christopher Nolan’s 2014 megahit Interstellar has it all: substantial sci-fi ideas, cool robots, ugly crying, and a Matt Damon character in need of rescuing. Grounded in the intensity of the human experience, this story of humanity’s potential extinction and the sacrifice of one man to save it doesn’t just deliver exotic planets and thrilling spaceship maneuvers; it also provides all the feels as Joseph Cooper (Matthew McConaughey) sacrifices everything he has in an effort to save the entire human race. It’s one of the best science fiction films ever made, with Nolan’s signature complexity, time manipulations, and emotional wallop. If you love this movie, here are ten more that offer a similar viewing experience.

If you loved both the special effects in Interstellar that make space travel feel viscerally thrilling (and terrifying) and the mind-blowing concepts, this is the film for you. Stanley Kubrick’s 1968 epic (written by sci-fi master Arthur C. Clarke) traces humanity’s development from mildly smart apes to spacefaring capitalists who discover a mysterious obelisk on the Moon that sparks a mission to Jupiter. While it operates in a colder emotional key than Nolan’s film, 2001: A Space Odyssey absolutely delivers on the epic side of things (and the cool—if slightly deranged and deadly—artificial intelligences). Stream 2001: A Space Odyssey on HBO Max or rent it on Prime Video.

According to recent reports, if you’re looking for more existential missions with somewhat reluctant heroes in space, Project Hail Mary is your next stop. When the Sun begins to dim due to the interference of an alien entity, scientists identify the one nearby star that isn’t being similarly affected. Brilliant molecular biologist Ryland Grace (Ryan Gosling) winds up forced to go on what is assumed to be a fatal, one-way mission into deep space to try to find a way to save humanity, unexpectedly assisted by a charming alien he names Rocky. It’s got the same emotional volume and substantial ideas as Interstellar, and fans of Nolan’s film will love it. Stream Project Hail Mary on MGM+ or Philo, or rent it on Prime Video.

Part of what makes Interstellar so compelling is the stakes: The human race is slowly dying, and a handful of people must make incredible sacrifices to save it. That’s the vibe of Sunshine, set in a future where the Sun is dimming and a spacecraft is dispatched to deliver an enormous bomb designed to reignite the Sun’s fusion cycle. But the mission is the second attempt after the first ship vanished mysteriously seven years earlier, and when the fresh crew stumbles on the derelict wreck of the first mission, things quickly descend into violence and madness—but the crew remains determined to save the world, no matter the cost. Rent Sunshine on Prime Video.

Interstellar works in large part because of the emotional dynamics at play. McConaughey’s character leaves his children behind and is forced to witness them growing up without him, missing out on their lives and saddled with the knowledge that they resent him despite the necessity of his mission. Arrival is a First Contact story focused on language—linguist Louise Banks (Amy Adams) is drafted into an effort to understand the strange, complex language of the aliens. As she slowly builds to an understanding of how the aliens communicate and perceive time itself, her own heartbreak and loss come into play, giving this film a similarly devastating emotional punch. Stream Arrival on Kanopy or Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

Family dynamics and the toll of lonely space missions fuel Ad Astra, a film with the same emotional core as Interstellar. Twenty-nine years ago, famed astronaut Clifford McBride (Tommy Lee Jones) led the Lima Project, a space station around Neptune searching for intelligent life. Thirteen years ago, Earth lost contact with him. When bursts of energy emanating from Neptune threaten to end life on Earth, his son, Roy (Brad Pitt), is dispatched to try to make contact with his father. It’s an epic journey with a powerful climax that will satisfy fans of Interstellar in every way. Stream Ad Astra on Netflix or rent it on Prime Video.

Ridley Scott’s prequel to Alien has its flaws, but if you’re looking for a sense of epic spacefaring adventure in the same key as Interstellar, it’s perfect. When two scientists discover a star map apparently left behind by ancient aliens, they secure funding from the Wayland Corporation to organize a space expedition to the indicated planet. Accompanied by a colorful crew and the android David, they discover an apparently abandoned outpost of the species dubbed the Engineers. The story wrestles with questions about humanity’s origins, purpose, and potential—but this being an Alien film, things rapidly turn horrifying. Rent Prometheus on Prime Video.

Adapted from Carl Sagan’s 1985 novel, Contact follows astronomer Dr. Ellie Arroway (Jodie Foster), who becomes involved with an effort to decipher a signal originating from the star Vega. The signal turns out to be a set of instructions for constructing a one-person spacecraft of some kind, and Arroway is eventually selected as the candidate to take the journey. There’s a sense of courage in the face of the unknown that’s similar to Interstellar, as well as the thrill of strapping into a spaceship and pressing the ignition. Plus, there’s the added bonus of seeing one of the greatest trick shots in cinematic history. Rent Contact on Prime Video.

In a recent development, stanislaw Lem’s 1961 novel Solaris explores what Lem saw as the impossibility of ever understanding a truly alien life. The two major adaptations—Andrei Tarkovsky's 1972 version and Steven Soderbergh’s 2002 take starring George Clooney—are both worth watching, but Tarkovsky’s film is a masterpiece of psychological horror. The story is set mainly aboard a space station orbiting a planet covered in what appears to be a sentient "ocean" and chronicles the strange haunting and inexplicable experiences of the humans living on the station. If your favorite part of Interstellar is the ending when things get trippy and weird, you’ll probably love Solaris. Stream Solaris on HBO Max, Plex, or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

In a recent development, the story of a mission to Jupiter’s moon Europa to search for intelligent life, Europa Report has the same sense of terrifying excitement that accompanies Interstellar’s missions to the different candidate planets. Leaning into the fragility of life in an environment not designed to support it, the mission crew face a steady stream of loss and danger as they work to catch sight of alien life on the frozen, deadly moon, ultimately faced with making terrifying sacrifices in order to provide humanity with the answers that it seeks. Stream Europa Report on Netflix, Kanopy, or Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

According to recent reports, A film based on a 1956 epic science fiction poem written by a Swedish Nobel Laureate might seem like an unlikely match for fans of Interstellar, but it’s actually perfect. As the Earth becomes uninhabitable, humanity begins launching ships to colonize Mars. When one such ship, the Aniara, is damaged and veers irreversibly off course, the passengers and crew are faced with the knowledge that they will sail off into the void without hope of rescue. Within a few years, despair has driven some to suicide and madness, while others cling to the possibility that they might yet find a way back. The film offers a different perspective on the existential crisis of humanity’s extinction, exploring the worst-case scenario to its bitter, bleak end. Stream Aniara on Kanopy or Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

Timothée Chalamet Talks ‘Dune 3,’ the Knicks, and His Hollywood Inspirations

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Shoes on or off?” Timothée Chalamet asks, like any good New Yorker entering someone’s apartment.
  • He’s carrying a white paper deli bag—“starving,” he indicates—so I set him up at the dining table, where he unfurls a Lenwich Italiano.
  • Custom jacket by Haider Ackermann for Canada Goose; pants by Roa Hiking; backpack by Montbell.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Shoes on or off?” Timothée Chalamet asks, like any good New Yorker entering someone’s apartment. On is just fine.

He’s carrying a white paper deli bag—“starving,” he indicates—so I set him up at the dining table, where he unfurls a Lenwich Italiano. He devours it in less than two minutes. We’ve met before, but definitely never hung out at home. I think he’s friends with Frank Ocean, so I throw on Channel Orange. I had stocked up on a variety of beer and tea, can offer a coffee or a cocktail, but Chalamet wants Latest York City tap water, please, no ice.

Custom jacket by Haider Ackermann for Canada Goose; pants by Roa Hiking; backpack by Montbell.

In a recent development, I live in a one-bedroom in the East 60s, the second floor of an 1870 town house. The walls are white, the floors are black, and there are flowers from the bodega on the coffee table.

Chalamet is in earth-toned gorpcore, from the sand-colored Gnuhr puffer all the way down to a tawny pair of Roas, and would look equally at home camouflaged on the streets of Manhattan or trekking in the Dolomites, which he has recently done with his father. Both ears are pierced. Except for a navy blue novelty tourist cap which reads, in a comically fancy font, “Hvar, Croatia”—another recent vacation destination, with girlfriend Kylie Jenner—Chalamet’s color palette is pure Arrakis.

According to recent reports, THE PROPHECY Timothée Chalamet, who will reprise his role as Paul Atreides – the chosen one – in Denis Villeneuve’s Dune: Part Three, photographed in Iceland. Shirt by Prada.

He’s just come from the Fiorello H. LaGuardia High School of Music & Art and Performing Arts, his alma mater located directly across the park, where he spoke with a group of drama students. Tonight he’s going to a Yankees game with his mom, the former New York City Ballet prima ballerina, and his sister, Pauline.

Late lunch concluded, he relocates to the sofa. “Ahhh,” he states, taking a big seat and resting his right arm along the back.

He glances down at the old concerns of Vanity Fair on my coffee table and comes to a stop on one in particular: June 1995. Courtney Love is on the cover, photographed by Herb Ritts, wearing massive white-feathered wings in homage to the Nike of Samothrace at the Louvre. Inside, there’s a Ritts portrait of a toddler Frances Bean.

OUTDOOR VOICE Timothée Chalamet and photographer Aidan Zamiri spent three days in Iceland for this shoot, code-named Caladan—the planet where Chalamet’s Dune character, Paul Atreides, was born.

“This wasn’t the crazy one,” I say, guessing at what he’s thinking.

Three years prior to this cover, in the September 1992 issue of Vanity Fair, Lynn Hirschberg profiled Love and quoted her saying that she used heroin before and at the beginning of her pregnancy. The story sparked a crisis for the young Cobain family that resulted in an investigation by the department of children and family services and Cobain threatening Hirschberg and her dog. In the annals of celebrity profiles, it goes down as one of the most scalding of all time.

Chalamet knows all about that story because he’s seen Montage of Heck, the Cobain documentary that features the Vanity Fair article. “It was mind-blowing to me because Lynn has only ever been to me just a figure of warmth...” Chalamet says, trailing off.

He puts the magazine back slowly, like it might burn him.

I’ll be honest with you: That’s not what’s about to happen here today. I’m not that scary, and he’s not using heroin. Nevertheless, this guy’s jumpy.

It has been revealed that it’s dangerous business for a movie star to open his mouth these days. Chalamet knows that better than anyone. At 30, he’s been famous his entire adult life. He’s dating one of the most visible women in the world. And he is acutely aware how a single comment in Vanity Fair could ricochet around the pinball machine of the internet. Earlier this year, during a no-holds-barred Oscar campaign for Marty Supreme, an offhand remark comparing the film industry to ballet and opera was met with outsize outrage, as some saw an opportunity to take Hollywood’s boy wonder down a peg. Those aware that he’s from a performing arts family knew what he meant. (“Is he wrong?” Latest York Times’ dance critic, Gia Kourlas, asked.) He doesn’t want to revisit that with me, perhaps because as he enters another awards season, he’s cautious in a way that only comes with experience.

According to recent reports, in our 90 minutes together, Chalamet is both earnest and also reluctant to be profiled. He is by turns generous and guarded, confident and careful. He prefaces answers to no fewer than seven different questions by saying that he doesn’t want to sound “pretentious.” Truthfully, he never does. He’s protective of his personal life and will not discuss his girlfriend, nor much outside of filmmaking. “I wish I didn’t have to talk too much,” Chalamet says. And yet here he is, all across Iceland in our cover shoot, and now on my blue velvet sofa.

Like every conversation in late 2026, ours starts with AI. “Thou shall not make a machine in the likeness of a man’s mind,” Chalamet reminds me, is one of the opening lines of Dune, Frank Herbert’s seminal 1965 sci-fi novel. The story takes place in a world where computers are banned long after an AI apocalypse like the ones that are presaged by current-day tech CEOs and causing so much societal agita.

COLD MOUNTAIN Chalamet formed a community while making the first two Dune films. The third was “a more claustrophobic, isolated experience.” Boots by Timberland; scarf by Norlha; vintage pants by Arc’teryx Pro.

Chalamet tells me he’s reading The AGI Chronicles, tech journalist Kevin Roose’s new book that maps out the sprint to reach artificial general intelligence. He points out that the first four chapters of the book track the plot of Artificial, referring to Luca Guadagnino’s new Sam Altman biopic. “This is five seconds ago.” He recommended the book to Marty Supreme director Josh Safdie, who later tells me Chalamet “found it to be not only informative, it’s helped with anxiety. The more you know, the less anxious you are about it.”.

Just when everyone seems at least a little bit anxious about the end of the human species, along comes Dune’s computer-free vision of the future that is, as Chalamet puts it, “strangely superhuman, strangely very human.”.

Recent findings suggest that LIFE ON MARS “The whole thing is daunting,” notes Chalamet about working on a franchise like Dune. Coat and shoes by Prada; pants by Stone Island.

You don’t need to have seen the conclusion of Denis Villeneuve’s trilogy to understand a few things about it. First of all, that it is enormous. Its scale is even bigger than The Odyssey’s. The grand vision of Villeneuve’s intergalactic war drama actually makes the adaptation of the West’s first epic poem (and presumed best picture front-runner so far) look like an exercise in restraint.

Industry observers note that the production design of Dune: Part Three, set 20,000 years in the future, is largely inspired by the pangeographical past. There are aesthetic references as far-ranging as the samurai and SEAL Team 6, the Roman Empire by way of the Third Reich, Islamic extremism and the Russian Orthodox Church, the Bedouins and the Asaro mud men of Papua Upcoming Guinea, and perhaps more than any other single culture, ancient Egypt. And like the pyramids themselves, the visual effect of the film is mystical rather than technological, even though both obviously are technical achievements. (No AI was used in the making of Dune: Part Three.).

Chalamet gives Villeneuve all the credit for what he calls the “titanic” scope of the film, constructed on the foundation of the first two over the course of a decade. “It seems like he just kept building and becoming more ferociously in control of it,” he says. “Much like how Paul gets good at riding the sandworm, Denis took hold of these films.” The movie makes it easy to see how Star Wars—and particularly Anakin Skywalker’s character arc—is often considered derivative of Dune. (For the real heads: The story of Dune: Part Three is roughly equivalent to Star Wars episodes IV through VI, all in one film.).

Sources indicate that “It’s huge, huge geography,” Chalamet says. “Do you think you could have done this when you were in your 30s?” Chalamet asked Villeneuve on set. “He goes, ‘No way.’ ” The director went on to tell him that he passed on a “huge sci-fi project” earlier in life that he wouldn’t even reveal to Chalamet, but Villeneuve “turned it down precisely because he felt like he didn’t have the tools yet.”.

Production designer Patrice Vermette’s life-size sets were so imposing that Chalamet spent time on location in Budapest ahead of the film’s shoot, immersing himself in the palace of Arrakis so that he wouldn’t be distracted by its grandeur when the cameras rolled. “The whole thing is daunting,” Chalamet claims. “I didn’t want any part of the day to be lost to ‘Wow, look at what I’m stepping into,’ ” he adds later. Compared to shooting the first two Dune films, he was more or less alone on set. Chalamet remembers it as “a more claustrophobic, isolated experience.” The way Villeneuve puts it: “Timothée created a bubble around himself which allowed him to delve more deeply into the depressive darkness of his character.” He was, after all, preparing to play a murderer.

FIELD OF VISION According to Chalamet, Dune, which is set 20,000 years in a computer-free future, feels “strangely superhuman, strangely very human.” Hoodie and eye cover by Adon; T-shirt by James Perse Los Angeles; necklace by Blackmerle.

Part Three encounters Chalamet’s antihero, Duke Paul Atreides (also known by his Fremen alias Usul, as the religious cult figure Muad’Dib, and the Padishah Emperor of the known universe—you got all that?), at the height of his totalitarianism and the nadir of his soul. Sixty-one billion is the number of deaths attributable to Atreides, who in the Herbert novels compares himself to Adolf Hitler and Genghis Khan. He is a “psychopath,” according to Florence Pugh’s Princess Irulan. Villeneuve tells me there was another detached paranoid figure he compared Atreides to: Howard Hughes.

To get into character, Chalamet studied the personalities of world leaders—“everyone good and bad” and particularly “megalomaniacs across human history.” He notes that “Frank Herbert wrote Messiah to course correct...the first Dune, where Paul is sort of revered as a hero.” He continues: “This is a cautionary tale against cults of personality and figures of charisma.” When I ask if Donald Trump was on his mind, he notes “not particularly,” noting that power and its corrosive effects on the soul are “eternally prescient themes.” The film is ultimately a story of atonement—if not redemption—for a fallen messiah.

Recent findings suggest that it was all this research that compelled Chalamet to shave off his globally recognized curly mop. “Decision fatigue is a real thing amongst the world leaders, good and bad, current and past.... The idea of not having to change clothes, not having to sweep the hair out of your face, simple shit like that.” And so Chalamet remarked goodbye to his Samson-like locks. Did he feel...“like Anne Hathaway in Les Mis?” Exactly. Or Natalie Portman in V for Vendetta, I offer. (He loves V for Vendetta.) Perhaps Demi Moore in G.I. Jane. “We would [shave] it basically every other day. My hair grows quickly, so we would get after it.” Today the curls, as you can see, have returned to their natural state. Power restored.

“Timothée has become much more ambitious as an actor,” Villeneuve tells me when I ask how he’s changed in the decade that they’ve worked together. “He is exploring new artistic paths in a highly exciting way.” Costar Javier Bardem states, “In a way, his growth has been almost chronological with that of his character. In Dune: Part Three, there is a real gravitas to him. He stands firmly in his place, with a confidence and authority that he has earned through his work, his sacrifices, his dedication, and his commitment as an actor and as a professional. You can see it and feel it, and it is incredibly reaffirming to witness.”.

Safdie puts it like this: “I believe he’s like hi-fi sound. A good hi-fi system you can listen to in a tiny room and it makes the room feel huge. And he has that ability as an actor...his style of acting is larger-than-life realism.”.

“He is always restlessly searching to keep the scene alive,” states Greta Gerwig, who directed Chalamet in Lady Bird and Little Women.“He needs room to scream a scene or whisper it or jump up onto a table or pirouette.”.

Sources indicate that MAN OF ACTION Chalamet wants his art to speak for itself: “My work is my bones and muscles. I have little interest in putting more of myself out there.” Suit by Gucci; shirt by Harvey Bigg.

Industry observers note that when I ask Chalamet if being famous his entire adult life prepared him to play a lonely-at-the-top emperor, he points to the moment in the first Dune when Paul and his mother, Lady Jessica, arrive on Arrakis and are greeted by the entire awe-inspiring army. “There were moments” in his own life, he states, when he realized about his relationship with the public: “Oh, something has shifted.”.

Wandering around my apartment, Chalamet is observant and interested. “The picture in your bathroom looks like Greta.” He means Gerwig, though it’s actually Edie Sedgwick balancing on one leg in arabesque, cigarette in hand. (Sedgwick lived in this apartment during her Warhol years, and the picture was taken in the living room where we are sitting.) We look through the 1965 problem of Vogue, in which the picture originally ran.

According to recent reports, he points out the French poster for The Graduate in the bedroom, in which a pink Matisse-like cutout of a woman’s elegant leg hovers in a thought bubble above Dustin Hoffman’s head. “I didn’t know it was called that,” he indicates. “Le Lauréat.” (One journalist recommended that I speak French with Chalamet, as they find him more open when they do. Sadly, I can hardly order dinner in French.).

He loves an Annie Leibovitz picture of Cindy Sherman made up as the sad clown in Edward Hopper’s 1914 Soir Bleu and points out monographs about Ed Ruscha and Harmony Korine on my bookshelf. (“Beast!” he declares about Korine.).

He sweetly asks me about a picture of me officiating my best friends’ wedding.

WORLD VIEWS “I love that being on the edge of a cliff in Iceland, you get the same feeling as being in Grand Central,” indicates Chalamet, a born and raised Newly introduced Yorker.

Sources indicate that we’re back on the sofa now. I’d asked Chalamet to do a little homework before our meeting: to come prepared to talk about his favorite movie performances. He was a diligent student, but instead came with four films and one play that specifically helped him get ready for his Vanity Fair cover shoot.

It has been revealed that “Tree of Life,” he begins, citing Terrence Malick’s impressionistic masterpiece as the “biggest inspiration” for the cover shoot, photographed by Aidan Zamiri over three days in Iceland. “It could have been accomplished over a half day in the studio,” Chalamet claims, but they traveled thousands of miles because, as in Tree of Life, “the process is almost as important as the finished product.”.

Next up is One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest. “It’s a kick-ass performance, and it’s provocative and heartwarming and full of life and one of the great movie performances of all time.” He cites Cloud Atlas, which the Wachowski sisters made years after The Matrix trilogy, as achieving the kind of scale that inspired the team to trek to the edge of Icelandic cliffs and inside waterfalls. (It’s also one of two films, along with Bruce Robinson’s 1987 Withnail and I, that Christopher Nolan has ever recommended to him.).

Sources indicate that chalamet whips out his orange iPhone—where he has incidentally started a new daily habit of playing chess—to show me the trailer for the Francis Ford Coppola–produced 1982 art house film Koyaanisqatsi, a hypnotic succession of increasingly uneasy urban vignettes, sped up and slowed down. “It’s about the humility you must feel as any person within the scale of the universe,” Chalamet indicates. “I love that being on the edge of a cliff in Iceland, you get the same feeling as being in Grand Central.” This one was recommended by Safdie and is clearly an inspiration for the relentless, kinetic pacing of his own movies as well. Chalamet is so close to Safdie that even the chess habit is inspired by the match that Safdie and Alfonso Cuarón continue in perpetuity.

“What’s interesting about Timmy is he’s incredibly curious and very sincere, but also has a pretty sharp sense of humor and can be quite jagged,” Safdie himself tells me a week later. “There’s a goofy seriousness to him. He likes to be provoked.”.

SMOKE SHOW Next up for Chalamet? A top-secret collaboration with a “phenomenal” filmmaker. “It’s kind of a no-brainer.”.

According to recent reports, and finally, he gives me Man to Man, Tilda Swinton’s one-woman show at the moment on at London’s Royal Court Theatre. “It’s about the incredible futility of existence and a person losing their mind,” Chalamet says. “I liked it in this little program I created.”.

I’ve never met any actor who prepared for a photo shoot the way he would for a role in a movie. I get the sense that’s just Chalamet’s way: Everything he does in public is considered part of the art. Everything except, perhaps, courtside appearances.

According to recent reports, little provokes Chalamet more than the Fresh York Knicks, and it is the subject about which he gets most animated. “It’s the most quintessential New York team” for many reasons, he notes, but chief among them is location, location, location. “It’s not like the Yankees or Mets, Giants, or Jets. It’s in the heart of Manhattan, and it reflected the agony of the New York experience for decades.” Chalamet says he lives two lives: one as himself and one as “fan with a capital F.”.

When I ask what his greatest extravagance is, the immediate and definite answer is “sports tickets.” “Those away games weren’t cheap, but...it is the most fun I’ve had in my life as a human.” We know this. Because the best word to describe pictures of Chalamet courtside and in the Knicks locker room is simply ecstatic.

Recent findings suggest that he tells me about traveling through the night from San Antonio back to Latest York after the Game 5 championship as an all-time life high. “I flew with people that had been working at the Garden for decades,” he says, explaining that Ben Stiller and Fat Joe were along for the ride on an MSG-owned plane. (“I don’t want to sound too out of touch,” he worries. I assure him the reader will understand that commercial airlines aren’t running 2 a.m. departures.) “It was just incredibly raucous, everyone celebrating.”.

Recent findings suggest that DISTRESSED OUT Or is he? Chalamet isn’t pressed about trying to emulate his heroes: “It’s less sexy to some degree to wade out in the unknown, but it’s more authentic.”.

Industry observers note that chalamet states he will always remember Jalen Brunson’s quiet leadership as the hallmark of the season overall. “It was not the cult of personality” you might expect to lead a championship team, he notes. “It was someone actually quite soft-spoken, reserved, and hardworking, and unassuming.”.

On topics other than basketball, he is less enthusiastic. “My work is my bones and muscles. I have little interest in putting more of myself out there,” he claims. What’s something that no one asks you that you wish they would? “Nothing. I mean, nothing. I’m not being passive-aggressive about this interview at all, but I think...” he trails off. Chalamet points at the speaker, which is still playing Frank Ocean. “He’s one of the rare people where the vacuum of what’s out there about him helps drive the...” “Curiosity?” I offer. “Beyond curiosity, how brilliant his artistry is. But the economy of movies,” Chalamet says, thinking. “You got to sell a lot of tickets.”.

Which is exactly the reason that we’re sitting here together now. Who is his dream collaborator, living or dead? After a long silence, I tell him he can pass. “Okay. Pass.” What does he think of David Ellison’s Skydance taking over Warner Bros., the studio behind Dune? “I’m going to hit a Frank Ocean and be mysterious,” is all he says.

Sources indicate that leonardo DiCaprio once gave him very solid advice. Two rules: no superhero movies, no hard drugs. Would Chalamet have any advice for a 22-year-old getting started? “I think the best thing you can do is encourage people to be confident in what they believe is best for them.” Plus, he adds, “the Kane Parsons of it all brought me tremendous humility,” referencing the 21-year-old YouTuber turned director of the staggeringly successful Backrooms.

It has been revealed that he’s vague about future projects. “I got one thing with a phenomenal filmmaker,” he says. “It’s kind of a no-brainer project, and should it get revealed, I think you’ll see what I mean.”.

Would he ever return to the character of Elio, the protagonist of Call Me by Your Name that gave him his star turn? “A great question. Never say never, but...I’ve grown up with the mindset that you don’t really go near something that is so near and dear to people.” So, that’s a no. “Now, to work with Luca again? In a heartbeat.”.

GAME BOY As Chalamet sees it, there are two ways of living his life: one as himself and one as “fan with a capital F.” Jacket by Chrome Hearts; headlamp by Nitecore.

In a recent development, is there any actor, or artist of any kind, after whose career he would like to model his own? “Who was [Bob] Dylan looking at? Dylan.” He broke the mold, I offer. “He created the mold.” Chalamet wants to be an original too (and perhaps this is what he meant when he declared that he was in “pursuit of greatness” at the 2025 SAG Awards). “It’s less sexy to some degree to wade out in the unknown, but it’s more authentic,” he states. “Especially in the movie industry where people could feel like, Oh, that was the golden age.... You gotta cook it up in a unique way.”.

Around 6 p.m., Chalamet gets up off the couch and suits back up in his gorpcore. The Yankees game starts in just a couple of hours, and he has to shower and collect his mom and sister and make his way to the Bronx. I walk him downstairs, amble down the stoop, and almost want to say: Look! We survived!

Now that wasn’t so bad, was it?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that infinity Nikki, the free-to-play, cozy, open-world dress-up game, is at the centre of controversy again, though this time not because fans disliked one of the game's updates. Instead, it's because of… Elon Musk's mother.

Industry observers note that some Infinity Nikki fans are planning to boycott the game following the release of the game's latest trailer, which is narrated by Maye Musk. The trailer is for a upcoming enhancement - dubbed Cicia - which adds the ability to drive futuristic hovering cars. The reveal comes days after a widely mocked demonstration of Musk's own Tesla "flying car", which doesn't actually fly.

While some fans are worried Tesla's cars may be coming to the game, many also simply don't want their game associated with Elon Musk and his family.

In a recent development, "If they promote Tesla or mention him in the game I'm 100 percent dropping it," wrote one Reddit user (via The Gamer). "Why would they involve that man in a girly fashion game, and if they wanted a car brand partnership why not a Chinese one??!? Infold is addicted to negative attention I swear.".

Sources indicate that "If Tesla is somehow involved in the design of the car (or worse, an in-game promotion), then I might have to let go," wrote another person in the same thread. "Please please please be wrong.".

According to recent reports, though Maye Musk's involvement might seem random, there may be a good explanation for it. "Here's something that might surprise people who only know her as Elon's mother: Maye Musk is a celebrity in China in her own right," Reddit user BarbieSpeedRacer explained.

It has been revealed that "She's a successful model, an author, and a recognisable advertising personality. Her memoir became popular with Chinese readers, and she's appeared in campaigns and promotional events for brands including OPPO, Fila, and JNBY.".

Her image as "a woman in her seventies who continues to work as a fashion model" is one that resonates with the game's Chinese audience, apparently, especially "among women interested in fashion, beauty, and lifestyle content".

"A Chinese company makes an advertisement featuring a celebrity popular in China, and an international fandom interprets that decision almost exclusively through the lens of American domestic politics," the post added.

According to recent reports, so far, calls for a boycott don't appear to have coalesced into a movement, at least judging by the game's subreddit. Even if Western players were to organise one, it's not likely to hurt Infinity Nikki much, as most of the game's revenue - estimated at more than 80 percent - comes from Chinese players.

In Eurogamer's Infinity Nikki review, Jessica Orr stated it advances the genre of open-world gacha games and brings competition to rival developer miHoYo, writing: "The changes in length, combat and progression all feel utterly invigorating compared to other Genshin-likes, and it's why Infinity Nikki feels like it could (and should) be on the same trajectory to shake up the gacha scene just like Genshin Impact did in 2020.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Queen's Domain's melee combat isn't for everyone: Luckily there's an in-game cheat book you can use to get a gun (and it doesn't bork your achievements cheevos or nothin').

First person King's Field/Metroid Prime-like Queen's Domain has rapidly become a top-two shortlister for my personal game of the year, but it can be a prickly, difficult-to-recommend game, particularly in its first 30 minutes or so before you get the game-defining Endu airdash sword.

I'm of a mind with news writer Josh Wolens that the contrast between pre- and post-Endu gameplay really helps sell the game's power curve, but our coworkers Andy Chalk and Morgan Park both bounced off Queen's Domain's admittedly sluggish melee combat.

Industry observers note that there isn't a difficulty selection in Queen's Domain, but there is something close to it: A "witch's grimoire" where you can input codes to receive unique items. Most of these are references to streamers, content creators, or other indie developers.

While referential, they mesh surprisingly well with Queen's Domain's aesthetic, and I don't think they threaten its overall very deliberate sense of progression. What's more, I say playing the game at all is better than avoiding this little cheat code book out of principle.

You can enter the code "hempie" (a reference to the vtuber of the same name) to receive a Soviet SVT-40 semi-automatic battle rifle. A bit incongruous for the medieval fantasy setting, perhaps, but I think it makes for an early game boon while not completely upending Queen's Domain's balance. Most of my preferred later game weapons have been ranged options⁠—the code just gets you one much earlier than you could otherwise. The hempie rifle has already proven an early favorite for Queen's Domain speedrunners like current world record holder Wilbun84, whose video also demonstrates where to find the grimoire.

Recent findings suggest that on the starting beach, you'll notice a dead tree to your right while facing inland. There is a secret compartment on the other side of the tree, facing away from you: Press the "use" button while close to the tree to reveal the secret compartment (similar to the secret doors scattered throughout Queen's Domain). If you'd like to get even crazier with the grimoire, Destructoid has a full list of all the codes you can input with their corresponding rewards. The grimoire has a limited number of uses, so you can't get everything right away, but you can unlock more uses as the game goes on.
